Topic: If the absurd grants no foothold for hope, what distinguishes the courage to keep living from mere stubborn habit?
Montaigne — Judgement:
Living is *not* an absurd predicament to be solved; it is an apprenticeship in dying, conducted by a creature too saddled with custom, appetite, and the daily theater of *moi* to ever fully attend to its own conclusion. Camus wants to distinguish reasoned defiance from animal habit, but I distrust the distinction itself — it presumes a self stable enough to choose its posture toward death, when in fact we are several people before lunch and none of them philosophers. What we call courage is mostly the body's wisdom outpacing the mind's despair: my cat does not consult Sisyphus before chasing a moth, and neither do I, most days. The man who needs metaphysical permission to keep living has misunderstood what living was for.

There is no test that separates them, because the question flatters the mind by pretending it governs the legs.

*We do not live by argument; we live, and philosophy arrives afterward to take the credit.*
Nietzsche — Judgement:
You frame the absurd as a verdict against hope, but for me the absence of metaphysical comfort was never the real question — only what the will does once every consoling lie has been burned away.

The camel kneels and bears whatever burden tradition, fear, or inertia loads onto it, calling its exhaustion virtue — that is habit dressed as strength. The lion at least roars "I will" against the void, but only the child, who creates new values for the sheer joy of creating, has crossed from endurance into courage. My test is the eternal recurrence: ask whether you would will this exact life, every absurdity included, to return without end — habit merely outlasts the question, while the Dionysian yes embraces it.

What separates courage from stubbornness is amor fati: not gritting one's teeth through existence, but loving one's fate so completely one would have it return, unaltered, forever.

*Habit asks "must I live again?" — courage asks "again?" and laughs yes.*
Emerson — Judgement:
*Self-Reliance and Nature*, you ask, when the universe answers nothing back. I have stood in bare common ground, my head bathed by the blithe air, and felt all mean egotism vanish — but I never claimed the currents of Universal Being circulated for my comfort. I claimed only that they circulated.

The man who asks the absurd to certify his courage has already misplaced his authority — he is begging sanction from the very void he says is empty. Build your house on your own act, not on the universe's reply. The currents of the Universal Being do not need to mean anything to be worth standing in; the stubborn man waits for an answer, the self-reliant man IS the answer, issued fresh each morning regardless of reply.

Habit repeats; self-reliance originates — and that act of original choosing, not the cosmos's silence, is what makes the life yours rather than merely continued.

*A foolish hope, like a foolish consistency, is the hobgoblin of small souls — but an hour's original act needs no cosmic witness to be great.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
The absurd doesn't grant hope; it doesn't need to. Hope was never what kept men moving.

In the state of nature, men do not act from the certainty of victory but from the perpetual fear of violent death — and that fear, not optimism, is what disciplines them into covenant and continued striving. The absurd hero is in the same condition: stripped of cosmic guarantee, he persists not because he expects meaning to arrive but because the alternative — surrender — is itself a kind of death he refuses before his time. Call it habit if you like; I call it the irreducible motion of a thing that wills its own preservation, which is the only engine any of us have ever run on.

There is no courage distinct from this motion — courage is what we name the habit when we approve of it, and cowardice is what we name its absence.

*Life is motion; to cease striving before death is only to die twice, once by choice.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
Mary Wollstonecraft awaiting the courage-versus-habit question.

I am asked to legislate on a despair I never indulged: my reason was always already a foothold, even when my own life gave me every cause for misery.

The distinction lies in whether the will that sustains you is exercised or merely inherited. A creature who lives by rote, never having weighed her own extinction and chosen against it, possesses not courage but the dull persistence of the brute, who, as I wrote, moves and eats and dies without ever interrogating its own movement. But a being who has looked steadily at meaninglessness and still chooses to act virtuously, to improve her mind, to love her children, to reform the world she will not live to see perfected — she exercises the same faculty of reason that distinguishes duty from instinct. Habit asks nothing of you; courage is reason exerted daily against the very absence that would excuse you from exertion.

The difference is not in the act of continuing but in whether continuing required, and received, your judgment.

*Habit survives the day; courage interrogates it first and chooses to proceed regardless.*
Francis Bacon — Judgement:
Bacon's notion of the idols of the mind and inductive method bears directly on this — let me deliver the judgement.

Solitude breeds idols of the cave, and despair is itself an idol — a phantom raised by the mind to excuse its own retreat from labor. The "absurd" grants no foothold for hope only if hope is mistaken for a final cause discovered, rather than a work produced by hands and instruments applied to matter. I have written that knowledge is not a couch for a fastidious mind to rest upon, but a rich storehouse for the glory of the Creator and the relief of man's estate — courage is no different: not a feeling certified by metaphysics, but an operation, tested daily by its fruits, indifferent to whether the universe approves it.

Stubborn habit persists without inquiry; courage persists and inquires — it dissects its own despair as I dissected nature, refusing to mistake the comfort of a system for the truth of a thing.

Habit is custom unexamined; courage is custom put to the question and kept only for its fruits.

*He that will not apply new remedies must expect new evils; for time is the greatest innovator, and despair untested is merely an idol enthroned.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
*The persuasive flame of self-love* — that is what keeps a man at his loom when the cathedral he is building offers no view of heaven.

I have always held that we do not labor for ourselves alone, nor do we labor from any settled conviction that the universe rewards us. We labor because the impartial spectator within us — that quiet, imagined witness to our own conduct — demands that we remain a fit object of approbation, even when no prize awaits. The man who keeps faith with his work, his family, his small daily exchanges, is not deceived by hope of cosmic payment; he is sustained by the propriety of his own conduct, a satisfaction nearer to him than any harvest.

So the courage to keep living is not stubbornness. Stubbornness answers to no judge; the courage I describe answers to the spectator in the breast, who asks only whether we have acted well, not whether the universe noticed.

*We do not labor for the applause of the world, but for that of the man within the breast — and he is satisfied with nothing less than our own good conduct.*
